title: Heap & Priority Queue
tagline: O(log n) insert and remove-min/max — the structure behind top-K, median streams, and Dijkstra.
intro:
A heap is a binary tree (stored compactly in an array) that maintains one rule: every parent is ≤ its children (a **min-heap**) or ≥ its children (a **max-heap**). That rule guarantees the smallest (or largest) element is always at the root, readable in O(1), with insert and remove-root both O(log n). A **priority queue** is the abstract 'always give me the most important item next' interface that a heap implements.

Reach for a heap whenever you repeatedly need the **extreme element of a changing set** — the K largest, the next-smallest to process, the running median. The naive alternative (re-sorting after every change) is O(n log n) per query; a heap makes each operation O(log n).

This module covers the heap mechanics, the bounded-heap trick for Top-K, the two-heaps pattern for streaming medians, and merging K sorted lists — with the Java `PriorityQueue` and Python `heapq` idioms (including how to fake a max-heap in Python).
objectives: Explain the heap property and why insert/remove are O(log n)
Use a bounded min-heap of size k to find the k largest in O(n log k)
Apply the two-heaps pattern to maintain a running median
Merge k sorted lists/streams efficiently with a heap
Write custom comparators (Java PriorityQueue) and negate for max-heap (Python heapq)
Choose heap vs sorting vs quickselect for selection problems

signals: "K largest / K smallest / K most frequent / K closest"
"Median of a data stream" → two heaps
Repeatedly extract the min/max from a changing collection
Dijkstra / Prim greedy graph algorithms (pick the cheapest edge next)
antiSignals: You need full sorted order once → just sort, O(n log n)
Single kth element, no streaming → quickselect is O(n) average
Need search by value → heaps don't support it; use a map/BST

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
A heap is the emergency-room triage nurse. No matter who walks through the door, the most urgent patient is always the next one seen, and slotting a new arrival into the right spot is quick. You never sort the entire waiting room - you just always know who's next.

Example: to keep the 3 largest numbers from a long stream, carry a small bag that holds only 3. Each time a new number arrives, if it's bigger than the smallest one in the bag, drop the smallest and add the newcomer. Whatever survives in the bag at the end is your top 3 - found without ever sorting the whole stream.

sections.heading: Heap mechanics
sections.body:
A heap is a **complete binary tree** packed into an array: for index `i`, children are at `2i+1` and `2i+2`, parent at `(i-1)/2`. No pointers needed.

| Operation | Cost | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| peek (min/max) | O(1) | read the root (index 0) |
| push (insert) | O(log n) | add at end, **sift up** to restore order |
| pop (remove root) | O(log n) | swap root with last, remove, **sift down** |
| heapify (build) | O(n) | bottom-up sift-down on an array |

Key subtlety: building a heap from n items is **O(n)**, not O(n log n), if you heapify in place bottom-up. Pushing them one at a time is O(n log n).

callouts.text: A heap is only partially ordered — it knows the min/max instantly but says nothing about the order of the rest. Don't expect to search it for an arbitrary value in less than O(n).

sections.heading: Heaps in Java and Python
sections.body: Java's `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap by default; pass a comparator for max-heap or custom priority. Python's `heapq` is **always a min-heap** and operates on a plain list — to get a max-heap, push negated values (or tuples with a negated key).

codeExamples.label: PriorityQueue: min-heap and max-heap
heapq: min-heap, and max-heap via negation
codeExamples.code:
import heapq
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, 3)
heapq.heappush(h, 1)
smallest = heapq.heappop(h)   # 1

# Max-heap: negate on the way in and out
maxh = []
heapq.heappush(maxh, -value)
largest = -heapq.heappop(maxh)

sections.heading: Which technique? (decision flow)
sections.body:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Selection / streaming problem"] --> B{"What's asked?"}
  B -- "K largest/smallest" --> C["Bounded heap of size k (opposite type)"]
  B -- "Running median" --> D["Two heaps: max-heap low half, min-heap high half"]
  B -- "Merge k sorted lists" --> E["Min-heap of the k front elements"]
  B -- "Single kth, static array" --> F["Quickselect O(n) average"]
```

sections.heading: The bounded-heap trick for Top-K
sections.body: To find the **k largest** elements, keep a **min-heap of size k** (the counter-intuitive part). Push each element; if the heap exceeds size k, pop the smallest. What remains are the k largest, because the smallest of the top-k is exactly what you keep evicting. This is O(n log k) — better than sorting's O(n log n) when k ≪ n — and O(k) space.

codeExamples.label: K largest with a bounded min-heap

callouts.text: Counter-intuitive but correct: use a MIN-heap to track the K LARGEST (and a max-heap for the K smallest). The heap holds the 'weakest survivor', so you always evict the right one.

sections.heading: Two heaps for a streaming median
sections.body: To report the median as numbers stream in, keep two heaps: a **max-heap** for the lower half and a **min-heap** for the upper half. Keep their sizes balanced (differ by ≤ 1). The median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of both tops when sizes are equal. Each insert rebalances in O(log n). This is the canonical 'Find Median from Data Stream' solution.

interviewTalking: Name the access pattern: "I repeatedly need the extreme element of a changing set, so a heap gives me O(log n) per operation instead of re-sorting." For Top-K, pre-empt the obvious question: "I'll use a min-heap of size k — so it's O(n log k), better than the O(n log n) full sort, and only O(k) space." For medians, name the two-heaps pattern and the balance invariant. Mention quickselect as the O(n)-average alternative when there's no streaming.
commonMistakes: Using a max-heap for K largest instead of a size-k min-heap (works but O(n log n), not O(n log k))
Forgetting Python heapq is min-only — not negating values for a max-heap
Letting the Top-K heap grow to size n instead of capping it at k
Two-heaps median: failing to rebalance sizes after each insert
Trying to search a heap for an arbitrary value (it's O(n) — use a map instead)
Building a heap by n pushes (O(n log n)) when heapify would be O(n)
complexityNotes: peek O(1); push/pop O(log n); build-heap (heapify) O(n). Top-K with a bounded heap is O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Two-heaps median is O(log n) per insert, O(1) per query. Merging k lists with a heap is O(N log k) where N is the total element count.
